summary: Specifies the Mail Transfer Protocol, an early way for hosts to deliver mail to one another. It was a step toward the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol that came later. Replaced by RFC 780.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 772 is a first draft of a protocol for transferring mail between hosts. A sender and receiver use one control connection for commands, replies and message text; RFC 780 later replaced this draft.

questions: what was the mail transfer protocol
how did mtp send a message
subtitle: A draft protocol for sending mail between network hosts

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a protocol to transfer mail to another host and receive clear results for each command.
tldr.mechanism: A sender opens a TELNET-based control connection, exchanges commands and numeric replies with the receiver, and sends mail over that same connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 772 is a first draft and was later replaced by RFC 780.

today: RFC 772 is a first draft and has been obsoleted by RFC 780.

sections.title: Sender, Receiver and Control Connection
sections.content:
The protocol has a sender-MTP process and a receiver-MTP process. The sender initiates a TCP or NCP control connection to the receiver's service port or socket 57. The connection follows TELNET rules and carries commands, replies and the mail itself.

The sender sends commands and interprets replies. The receiver interprets commands, returns replies and handles the mail. Mail is transferred as a stream of octets over the control connection, not a separate data connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending host connects to the receiving host and uses that connection for the whole exchange. It carries requests, answers and the message text.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
MTP commands are NVT-ASCII lines ending in CRLF. MAIL starts a mail transfer; HELP requests information; QUIT asks the receiver to close the connection; NOOP requests an OK reply. MRSQ selects a multiple-recipient scheme, and MRCP identifies recipients under that scheme.

Each command produces at least one reply. A reply has a three-digit code and text: programs use the code to determine what to do next, while the text is generally for a human. The first digit indicates preliminary, successful, intermediate, temporary failure or permanent failure status.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender issues a text command and waits for a numbered reply. Programs can act on the code, while people can read the accompanying explanation.

sections.title: Mail Text and Multiple Recipients
sections.content:
MTP represents mail as NVT-ASCII, converting between a host's internal character format and the common form. CRLF marks the end of a text line. The MAIL command supplies the sender and optional destination path; after the receiver accepts the mail, the sender transmits the text, ending it with CRLF, a period, and CRLF.

For several recipients at one host, MRSQ selects either recipients-first (R) or text-first (T), and MRCP identifies recipients. The RFC describes no recovery or restart procedure for major host or network failures; it says detection of lost or scrambled bits is handled by TCP or NCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol converts mail to a common text form and marks where each line and message ends. It also offers two ways to send one message to several recipients at the same host.
